concept.name: Episodic memory
concept.definition: The long-term memory of an agent's own past experiences: records of specific episodes — observations, actions taken, and outcomes — from earlier decision cycles or sessions. In the CoALA framework, episodic memory stores sequences of past events the agent can retrieve to inform current decisions, paralleling the cognitive-science distinction introduced by Tulving.
concept.intuition: The agent's diary: 'last Tuesday the user asked X, I did Y, and the result was Z' — specific events, retrievable later.
concept.mechanics: Each episode (or summarized version) is stored — often as text embedded in a vector store — and retrieved by similarity to the current situation. Retrieved episodes support few-shot-style recall of precedents, correction after past mistakes, and personalization across sessions.
concept.failure_modes: Similarity-based retrieval surfaces superficially similar but materially different past episodes, encouraging analogy errors; stale episodes keep influencing behavior after conditions change. Logging everything without summarization floods retrieval with noise.
concept.misconceptions: Episodic memory is not a transcript replay — retrieval is approximate and lossy. It is also not knowledge about the world: an episode records what happened to the agent, which may have been a mistake.
concept.example: An agent recalls that in a prior session it sized a natural-gas position using the wrong contract multiplier and was corrected; when a similar sizing request arrives, it retrieves that episode and checks the multiplier first.

citations.source: Sumers et al., 'Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)' (2023)
